catalog_quote: In these four languages the contrastive supra-segmental feature is not so much one of pitch levels or stress intensity as of syllable emphasis. That is, each language has one distinct supra-segmental phoneme which when it occurs gives con[trast] to affected syllables over neutral syllables. ... In KAMANO and BENABENA it is a phoneme of stress which contrasts with syllables which are unstressed. Examples: KAMANO ka'na "heavy" 'kana "road" ka'fa "rat" 'kafa "door" ka'rafee "she[ll]?" kara'tee "tree kangaroo" ... In KAMANO there is only one degree of intensity, of stress. A word has one or two stressed syllables. In compound words and in words of two syllables the placement of the second stress is not predictable from the first; but in all other words it is. sources.citation: Drew, Dorothy E. [1963] 2007. The phonemes of Kamano. Unpublished ms., Summer Institute of Linguistics, Ukarumpa. 15 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives; old SIL-PNG id 49241)
sources.quote: 'The phonological word ... has a nucleus of pertinent stress placement. This may fall on the first, second or third syllable.' 'Stress is shown by length and intensity. A stressed syllable is usually accompanied by higher pitch. There is one pertinent stress per phonological word from which others may be predicted. Non-pertinent stresses radiate on alternate syllables preceding and succeeding the pertinent stress.' Stress patterns listed for 2-4 syllable words ('-, -', '--, -'-, --' ...; e.g. noya' fish vs pasa' bamboo comb). Verbs: 'Pertinent stress falls on the penultimate syllable of verbs
sources.locator: sec. 6 'Phonological Word' and sec. 7 'Stress', ms pp. 6-11 (PDF pp. 8-13)

sources.quote: 'Stress is phonemic, but is not written. Examples: kaná 'heavy' / kána 'road'. Tone is predictable by stress. The stressed syllable is either mid or high tone.'

sources.quote: 'The Syllable in Kamano is a unit of potential stress placement'; 'The phonological word is a unit which may occur in isolation and which carries one pertinent stress. Up to eight syllables may combine to form a word.' No placement rule beyond this; defers to the phonemic statement.
